question:
Integers \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) satisfy

\[ \begin{aligned} ab + c &= 100, \\ bc + a &= 87, \\ ca + b &= 60. \end{aligned} \]

What is \(ab + bc + ca?\)
solution:
The first two right-hand sides differ by the prime number \(13\). Subtracting those equations creates a product of integers with very few possibilities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
13&=(ab+c)-(bc+a)\\
&=b(a-c)-(a-c)\\
&=(b-1)(a-c).
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(13\) is prime, \(b-1\) must be one of \(-1,1,13,-13\). We check all four cases.

- If \(b-1=-1\), then \(b=0\). The first two equations give \(c=100\) and \(a=87\), but the third would require \(ca=60\), which is impossible.
- If \(b-1=1\), then \(b=2\), \(a-c=13\), and \(ca=58\). The positive factor pairs of \(58\) are \((1,58)\) and \((2,29)\), with differences \(57\) and \(27\). Negative factor pairs have the same absolute differences, so none can satisfy \(a-c=13\).
- If \(b-1=13\), then \(b=14\), \(a-c=1\), and \(ca=46\). The positive factor pairs \((1,46)\) and \((2,23)\) have differences \(45\) and \(21\). Again, negative pairs have the same absolute differences, so this case is impossible.
- If \(b-1=-13\), then \(b=-12\), \(a-c=-1\), and \(ca=72\). Substituting \(a=c-1\) gives
\[
c(c-1)=72,
\qquad (c-9)(c+8)=0.
\]
Thus \((a,c)=(8,9)\) or \((-9,-8)\). The first pair fails the first equation because \(8(-12)+9=-87\). The second pair works:
\[
108-8=100,\qquad96-9=87,\qquad72-12=60.
\]

All possible integer cases have been checked, so \((a,b,c)=(-9,-12,-8)\). Therefore
\[
ab+bc+ca=108+96+72=\boxed{276},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
